language.script_notes: French as the official/signage language, a legacy of French colonial rule; Wolof is the widely spoken lingua franca in daily life though rarely on formal signage. Street suffixes: Rue, Avenue, Boulevard, Place, Quartier.
false_friends: Gambia (a country entirely surrounded by Senegal)

road_furniture.bollard_color: Bollards are rare overall; where present, some resemble standard French-style posts, with a distinct pattern occasionally seen around curves in the southeast.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: Inconsistent/rare — absence of bollards is itself a mild tell versus France.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: Minimal; often absent on rural roads.
road_furniture.line_paint: White outside/white inside lines, often faded from heat and wear.
road_furniture.curb_style: Minimal formal curbing outside central Dakar/Saint-Louis; open sandy/dirt shoulders common.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Yellow-capped kilometer markers. Ladder-style utility poles, a legacy of French colonial infrastructure shared with parts of France. Total, Puma, Elton and Petrosen are common fuel-station brands.

architecture.roof_style: Simple flat or low-pitch roofs on most buildings; French colonial-era buildings in Dakar and Saint-Louis carry ornate wrought-iron balconies and large ventilation windows.
architecture.roof_material: Corrugated metal roofing widespread; colonial-era buildings sometimes carry tile.
architecture.wall_construction: Sun-dried mud brick construction traditional in the northern/central Sahel zone; laterite stone and colonial-style pastel-painted stucco in Saint-Louis and central Dakar; narrow-street courtyard housing with decorative wooden doors in Dakar's Medina district.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Pastel-painted French colonial facades in Saint-Louis; earthy mud-brick tones in the rural Sahel interior; more modern concrete-block construction in expanding Dakar.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: French colonial administrative buildings and pastel-facaded houses with wrought-iron balconies (Saint-Louis, central Dakar); mud-brick Sahelian village architecture; the Medina district's dense courtyard housing.

nature.vegetation: Baobab trees are a strong, near-iconic Senegal/Sahel tell, often marking villages from a distance; arid Sahel scrub and savanna grassland in the north/center, transitioning to lush, greener Casamance forest in the south near Guinea-Bissau.
nature.terrain: Mostly flat to gently rolling, with a long Atlantic coastline; the Senegal River forms the northern border with Mauritania; the Gambia River cuts through, with the entire country of Gambia forming an enclave within Senegal's territory.
nature.climate_signature: Hot and dry Sahelian climate in the north, increasingly humid and green moving south into Casamance — a noticeable within-country vegetation gradient.

vehicles.plate_color: Since 2019, black text on white with a blue country strip; older pre-2019 plates were white text on blue background.
vehicles.plate_format: Two-letter regional code plus digits (older format); current format follows a broadly similar regional-plus-serial structure.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Older French-brand vehicles (Renault, Peugeot) and shared 'car rapide' brightly painted minibus taxis are a strong Dakar-area tell.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Mixed — official Google coverage supplemented by Trekker imagery in less accessible areas.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Concentrated in and around Dakar and major towns; sparse coverage in rural/interior areas.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Gambia is a narrow country entirely surrounded by Senegal on three sides, sharing near-identical vegetation, architecture and climate
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Gambia is a former British colony and uses English on signage rather than Senegal's French, and Gambia drives on the right same as Senegal, so language/signage is the most reliable distinguishing detail.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared Sahel vegetation and mud-brick Sahelian architectural tradition, French colonial administrative language
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Mali is landlocked with no coastline, while Senegal has a long Atlantic coast; distinguishing them inland often comes down to plate format and subtler road-furniture details.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared Sahel/Sahara transitional vegetation and climate, shared Senegal River border
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Mauritania's official language is Arabic (with French also used), and Arabic script appears on Mauritanian signage — absent in Senegal, which uses French/Latin script only.
